advances:
This gives an affine-covariant exposed-edge inequality for the
extension-aware residual route.  A single transverse exposed face of
\(B_0\) spanning the two walls adjacent to a singleton chamber converts
a required added singleton area into explicit lower bounds for both
transverse added caps.  The resulting necessary inequality can be
substituted directly into the crossing algebra.  The statement also
identifies the exact applicability criterion and shows that containment
of the central triangle plus positivity of all seven cells does not by
itself supply the required spanning face.  The first remaining global
step is therefore a boundary-chain classification using the endpoint
Minkowski geometry.

proof:
The map \(x\mapsto(S,T)\) is an affine isomorphism because
\(\nabla f_2,\nabla f_3\) are linearly independent.  Its absolute
Jacobian is the reciprocal of \(\gamma\), proving the area conversion
in (5).  In these coordinates
\[
f_1=-1-\frac S\alpha-\frac T\beta,
\]
but only the signs \(S\geq0\Longleftrightarrow f_2\geq0\) and
\(T\geq0\Longleftrightarrow f_3\geq0\) are used below.

The vertex \(O=(0,0)\) of the central triangle belongs to \(B\) by
(1).  The segment in (4) contains \(U=(0,\varepsilon)\) and
\(V=(\varepsilon,0)\).  Hence convexity gives
\[
\operatorname{conv}\{O,U,V\}\subseteq B.
\]
Conversely, (3) shows that every point of \(B\) in the nonnegative
quadrant belongs to that same triangle.  This proves (9).

Put
\[
r=S+T-\varepsilon.
\]
By (9), every added singleton-\(1\) point has \(r>0\).  At a fixed
depth \(r\), the whole singleton chamber is the interval
\[
0<S<\varepsilon+r,\qquad T=\varepsilon+r-S,
\]
whose \(S\)-length is \(\varepsilon+r\).  The change
\((S,T)\mapsto(S,r)\) has determinant \(1\).  Integrating the maximal
possible cross-sectional length from \(0\) to \(R\), then multiplying
by \(\gamma\), proves (10).

Compactness gives a maximizer \(P\) in (8), proving (11).  Work first
in the \((S,r)\)-coordinates.  The three points
\[
F=(-A,0),\qquad U=(0,0),\qquad P=(S_P,R)
\]
belong to \(K\).  Their convex hull is contained in \(K\).  The segment
\([F,P]\) meets \(S=0\) at depth
\[
\frac{AR}{A+S_P}.
\]
Therefore the subtriangle of
\(\operatorname{conv}\{F,U,P\}\) in \(S\leq0\) has coordinate area
\[
\frac{A^2R}{2(A+S_P)}.
\]
Its interior has \(r>0\), while \(B\subseteq\{r\leq0\}\), so it is
added area.  Multiplication by \(\gamma\) proves the first inequality
in (12).  The proof of the second is identical in the coordinates
\((T,r)\), using
\[
E=(-C,0),\qquad V=(0,0),\qquad P=(T_P,R).
\]

Since \(S_P,T_P\leq\varepsilon+R\), (13) follows immediately.  For
(14), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
\frac{A^2}{A+S_P}+\frac{C^2}{C+T_P}
\geq
\frac{(A+C)^2}
{A+C+S_P+T_P}.
\]
Using (11) in the denominator and then (12) proves (14).  If one of
\(A,C\) is zero, omit its zero term before applying the same inequality;
if both vanish, (14) is \(e_2+e_3\geq0\).

The right side of (10) is increasing in \(R\geq0\).  Solving
\[
Z=\gamma\left(\varepsilon R+\frac{R^2}{2}\right)
\]
for its nonnegative root gives (15).  The function
\[
R\longmapsto
\frac{\gamma R(A+C)^2}
{2(A+C+\varepsilon+R)}
\]
is increasing, strictly so when \(A+C>0\).  Equations (10), (14), and
(15) therefore prove (16), including its strict form.

It remains to derive the crossing specialization.  Let
\[
d_i=|B\cap\{f_i\leq0\}|.
\]
The \(i\)-th crossing for \(K\), together with
\(|K|=|B|+\Delta\), reads
\[
u_i+v_i+d_i+e_i
=h_0+\frac{2\Delta}{9}.
\]
This is (18).  The added triple cell is null because its ambient
chamber is exactly \(\mathcal T\), already contained in \(B\).  If
\(S_{\rm add}\) and \(D_{\rm add}\) denote the total added singleton
and doubleton areas, then
\[
\Delta=S_{\rm add}+D_{\rm add},
\qquad
\sum_i e_i=S_{\rm add}+2D_{\rm add}.
\]
Summing (18) gives
\[
\sum_i e_i=\frac{2\Delta}{3}-G,
\]
and elimination of \(S_{\rm add}\) proves (19).

Writing \(z_{ij}\) for the added doubleton cells,
\[
e_1=z_1+z_{12}+z_{13},
\qquad
D_{\rm add}=z_{12}+z_{13}+z_{23}.
\]
Thus \(z_1\geq e_1-D_{\rm add}\), and substitution of (18)--(19)
proves (20).  Equations (16), (18), and (20) now give (21)--(22).

For the applicability claim, a supporting line whose outward normal is
a strict positive linear combination of the \(s\)- and \(t\)-wall
normals can be written in the form \(S+T=\varepsilon\) after the
positive diagonal scaling (2).  Such a face supplies both transverse
triangles exactly when it spans both axes, which is precisely (4).
Items 1--4 are therefore exactly the geometric and ledger hypotheses
used in the proof, while item 5 is exactly the contradiction to the
necessary conclusion (22).

For (23), direct edge-orientation tests place all three vertices of the
central triangle in \(B^\ast\).  Exact clipping by
\[
s=0,\qquad t=0,\qquad s+t=-1
\]
gives (24).  The counterclockwise vertex list in (23) shows that the
only exposed edges wholly on the outward singleton frontier are (25).
The adjacent edge from \((2,-5)\) to \((4,1/2)\) misses the \(s\)-axis,
and the adjacent edge from \((1/2,4)\) to \((-5,2)\) misses the
\(t\)-axis.  Hence no one exposed face spans both walls.  This proves
the claimed insufficiency of the \(B\)-only hypotheses.

Finally, all formulas are continuous at \(A=0\), \(C=0\), \(R=0\), and
\(\varepsilon=0\), with the stated zero-term convention.  If
\(\alpha=0\), an added point can move arbitrarily far in the
\(S\)-direction at fixed normal depth, making the triangle forced in
\(S\leq0\) arbitrarily small; the case \(\beta=0\) is symmetric.
Thus no positive two-cap estimate depending only on normal depth and
finite intercept data survives the parallel limit.  This proves all
listed degeneracy assertions.
statement:
Let \(f_1,f_2,f_3\) be nonconstant affine functions on
\(\mathbb R^2\), with pairwise nonparallel linear parts and
\[
f_1+f_2+f_3=-1.
\]
Let \(B\subseteq K\) be compact two-dimensional convex bodies and assume
\[
\mathcal T=\{f_1,f_2,f_3\leq0\}\subseteq B.
\tag{1}
\]
Focus on the singleton-\(1\) chamber and put
\[
s=f_2,\qquad t=f_3.
\]

Assume that \(B\) has one transversely spanning exposed face as follows.
There are \(\alpha,\beta>0\), \(\varepsilon\geq0\), and \(A,C\geq0\)
such that, in the affine coordinates
\[
S=\alpha s,\qquad T=\beta t,
\tag{2}
\]
one has
\[
B\subseteq\{S+T\leq\varepsilon\},
\tag{3}
\]
and the exposed face on the supporting line \(S+T=\varepsilon\) is the
segment with endpoints
\[
F=(-A,\varepsilon+A),\qquad
E=(\varepsilon+C,-C).
\tag{4}
\]
Thus the face contains the two wall intercepts
\[
U=(0,\varepsilon),\qquad V=(\varepsilon,0).
\]
Let
\[
\gamma=
\frac{1}
{\alpha\beta\,|\det(\nabla f_2,\nabla f_3)|},
\tag{5}
\]
so physical area equals \(\gamma\) times area in the
\((S,T)\)-coordinates.

Define the added transverse cap areas and the added singleton-\(1\)
area by
\[
e_2=|(K\setminus B)\cap\{S\leq0\}|,\qquad
e_3=|(K\setminus B)\cap\{T\leq0\}|,
\tag{6}
\]
\[
z_1=|(K\setminus B)\cap\{S>0,\ T>0\}|.
\tag{7}
\]
The maximal outward singleton depth is
\[
R=
\max\{S+T-\varepsilon:(S,T)\in K,\ S\geq0,\ T\geq0\}.
\tag{8}
\]
It is nonnegative because \(U,V\in B\subseteq K\).

Then the singleton section of \(B\) is exactly the triangle
\[
B\cap\{S\geq0,\ T\geq0\}
=
\{S\geq0,\ T\geq0,\ S+T\leq\varepsilon\},
\tag{9}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\quad
z_1\leq
\gamma\left(\varepsilon R+\frac{R^2}{2}\right).
\quad}
\tag{10}
\]

Choose a maximizer \(P=(S_P,T_P)\) in (8).  Thus
\[
S_P,T_P\geq0,\qquad S_P+T_P=\varepsilon+R.
\tag{11}
\]
With the convention that a term with zero numerator and zero
denominator is \(0\), convexity forces
\[
\boxed{\quad
e_2\geq
\frac{\gamma A^2R}{2(A+S_P)},\qquad
e_3\geq
\frac{\gamma C^2R}{2(C+T_P)}.
\quad}
\tag{12}
\]
In particular, the following bounds depend only on the edge data and
the maximal depth:
\[
\boxed{\quad
e_2\geq
\frac{\gamma A^2R}{2(A+\varepsilon+R)},\qquad
e_3\geq
\frac{\gamma C^2R}{2(C+\varepsilon+R)}.
\quad}
\tag{13}
\]
The stronger joint bound is
\[
\boxed{\quad
e_2+e_3
\geq
\frac{\gamma R(A+C)^2}
{2(A+C+\varepsilon+R)}.
\quad}
\tag{14}
\]

Equivalently, if a separate ledger gives \(z_1\geq Z\geq0\), define
\[
R_Z=
\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+\frac{2Z}{\gamma}}-\varepsilon.
\tag{15}
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{\quad
e_2+e_3
\geq
\frac{\gamma R_Z(A+C)^2}
{2(A+C+\varepsilon+R_Z)}.
\quad}
\tag{16}
\]
Strict \(z_1>Z\), together with \(A+C>0\) and \(Z>0\), makes (16)
strict.

For the crossing application, put
\[
h_0=\frac{2(M+m+|B|)}9,\qquad
\rho_i=u_i+v_i+|B\cap\{f_i\leq0\}|-h_0,
\qquad
G=\rho_1+\rho_2+\rho_3.
\tag{17}
\]
If \(K\supseteq B\) has added area
\[
\Delta=|K\setminus B|
\]
and satisfies the three crossings, then
\[
e_i=\frac{2\Delta}{9}-\rho_i.
\tag{18}
\]
Since (1) makes the added triple cell null, the total added doubleton
area is
\[
D_{\rm add}=-\frac{\Delta}{3}-G.
\tag{19}
\]
Consequently
\[
z_1\geq e_1-D_{\rm add}
=\frac{5\Delta}{9}+\rho_2+\rho_3.
\tag{20}
\]
Put
\[
Z_\Delta=
\left(\frac{5\Delta}{9}+\rho_2+\rho_3\right)_+,
\qquad
R_\Delta=
\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+\frac{2Z_\Delta}{\gamma}}
-\varepsilon.
\tag{21}
\]
Every crossing extension must satisfy the extension-aware residual
inequality
\[
\boxed{\quad
\frac{4\Delta}{9}-\rho_2-\rho_3
\geq
\frac{\gamma R_\Delta(A+C)^2}
{2(A+C+\varepsilon+R_\Delta)}.
\quad}
\tag{22}
\]

For a fixed endpoint model and a fixed \(\Delta\), the hypotheses needed
to obtain a contradiction from this lemma are exactly:

1. a singleton index whose ledger lower bound \(Z_\Delta\) in (21) is
positive;
2. a nonparallel exposed face with outward normal in the interior of
the cone generated by the two adjacent wall normals, equivalently
\(\alpha,\beta>0\) in (2);
3. that one face spans both adjacent walls, equivalently it has the
form (4);
4. positive transverse reach \(A+C>0\); and
5. strict reversal of (22).

To apply this one-face lemma to every dominant all-double endpoint
model, one must prove that every model surviving the scalar interval
gate has such an index and such a face, with parameters making item 5
hold.  The currently stated \(B\)-only hypotheses do not imply item 3.
Indeed, in the \((s,t)\)-plane consider the counterclockwise polygon
\[
B^\ast=\operatorname{conv}\left\{
(2,-5),\left(4,\frac12\right),
\left(\frac52,3\right),\left(\frac12,4\right),
(-5,2),(-3,-3)
\right\}.
\tag{23}
\]
It contains
\[
\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(-1,0),(0,-1)\}
\]
and its seven cell areas, indexed by the negative set of
\((f_1,f_2,f_3)=(-1-s-t,s,t)\), are
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_1&=\frac{1015}{88},&
b_2&=\frac{86}{15},&
b_3&=\frac{86}{15},\\
b_{12}&=\frac{1322}{165},&
b_{13}&=\frac{1322}{165},&
b_{23}&=\frac{121}{10},&
b_{123}&=\frac12.
\end{aligned}
\tag{24}
\]
All are positive.  Its exposed frontier through the singleton-\(1\)
chamber contains the two distinct edges
\[
\left[\left(4,\frac12\right),\left(\frac52,3\right)\right],
\qquad
\left[\left(\frac52,3\right),\left(\frac12,4\right)\right],
\tag{25}
\]
and no exposed face meets both axes.  Thus (1) and all-seven-cell
positivity give a polygonal singleton frontier, but not the single
spanning face (4).  Any universal application must either prove that
the dominant endpoint Minkowski structure excludes the multi-edge
frontier (25), or extend (12)--(16) from one face to a whole exposed
chain.

The boundary cases are as follows.

- If \(R=0\) or \(Z=0\), the corresponding lower bounds are \(0\).
- If \(A=0\) or \(C=0\), the relevant individual triangle in (12)
  degenerates and no positive lower bound for that cap follows.  The
  other term and the joint bound remain valid.  If \(A=C=0\), (14) is
  identically \(0\).
- The face in (4) has zero length exactly when
  \(\varepsilon=A=C=0\).  It is then an exposed vertex, and the lemma
  gives no transverse charge.
- If \(\alpha=0\) or \(\beta=0\), the supporting face is parallel to
  one adjacent wall.  There is no finite two-wall normalization (2)
  and no positive two-cap bound depending only on normal depth and
  finite edge intercepts.  A separate one-sided or tangential-width
  estimate is required.
